paragraphs: Optimal transport measures how closely two distributions match by finding a low-cost way to move mass between them. Combinatorial algorithms can compute this quantity, but their steps have been difficult to distribute across processors. This has encouraged numerical approaches that fit GPU computation more naturally.

The paper introduces a parallel combinatorial algorithm with an additive error guarantee: its estimate is within an error tolerance ε of the optimal transport distance. Its parallel complexity is O(log(n)/ε²), where n is the combined support size. For massive parallel computation, the authors also obtain an approximate transport plan with O(log(log(n/ε))/ε²) communication rounds and O(n/ε) memory per machine. Earlier algorithms in that setting require at least logarithmically many rounds in n.

The authors express the algorithm as matrix row and column operations, making its connection to GPU execution concrete. Experiments suggest faster performance than leading approximate GPU solvers, particularly for larger inputs. The contribution combines theoretical parallel guarantees with an implementation perspective; the observed speed advantage remains an empirical finding.
neurips-2023-a-combinatorial-algorithm-f.tldr: A parallel combinatorial optimal transport algorithm provides approximation guarantees and shows promising GPU speed advantages on larger inputs.

paragraphs: Machine learning researchers increasingly work on reproducing climate simulations, refining their spatial detail, and making predictions. Many existing datasets come from a single climate model, which limits opportunities to study how methods behave across different simulators. ClimateSet addresses the need for a consistent collection prepared for machine learning.

The dataset brings together inputs and outputs from 36 climate models in the Input4MIPs and CMIP6 archives. The authors also supply a modular pipeline for retrieving and preprocessing further models and scenarios. This makes the contribution both a usable collection and a way to extend that collection as research needs change.

The paper demonstrates ClimateSet through climate model emulation: training machine learning models to reproduce simulator outputs. Comparing performance across climate models provides insights into generalization. The collection also supports training one emulator on several simulators. Such a system can rapidly project additional climate scenarios, potentially complementing those available to policymakers. The broader promise is a shared basis for studying climate tasks across multiple models.
neurips-2023-climateset-a-large-scale-cl.tldr: ClimateSet assembles inputs and outputs from 36 climate models to support broader machine learning evaluation and climate emulation.

paragraphs: People can inspect the same scene with different goals, directing attention toward information that matters for the current task. Standard vision models often lack this flexibility. The paper adds long-range feedback connections inspired by cognitive and biological mechanisms, allowing a model's visual processing to respond to an internally specified goal.

The feedback originates in the final layer of the visual backbone. Goals are expressed as vectors in its output space, providing an interface for steering how the network processes an image. The connections modulate activity multiplicatively. The authors report that this design avoids rampant hallucination of the requested category, helping separate a search goal from the actual visual evidence.

Models with these pathways improve image recognition, adversarial robustness, and alignment with brain measurements relative to the baselines studied. Steering also substantially improves category recognition in composite images containing multiple categories, where the feed-forward baselines struggle. These results support feedback as a useful mechanism for goal-directed vision and as an interface through which cognitive goals can influence visual representations.
neurips-2023-cognitive-steering-in-deep-.tldr: Long-range feedback connections let vision models respond to goals while improving recognition and limiting goal-driven hallucination.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks which connections should exist in a graph. Incorrect or missing edges create a particularly difficult problem because edges serve two roles: they describe the structure supplied to the model and help define its prediction targets. The authors' empirical study shows that noise can therefore corrupt both inputs and supervision, sharply reducing performance and causing learned representations to collapse.

The proposed Robust Graph Information Bottleneck, or RGIB, addresses these two sources of corruption together. It separates and balances the dependencies among graph structure, target labels, and learned representations. This information-theoretic principle produces training objectives intended to retain reliable supervision while preventing the representation from losing useful distinctions.

The paper develops two implementations. RGIB-SSL uses self-supervised learning for implicit denoising, while RGIB-REP uses data reparameterization for explicit denoising. Experiments cover six datasets, three graph neural networks, and varied noise scenarios, supporting both implementations. The main contribution is treating noisy topology and noisy labels as a coupled learning problem.
neurips-2023-combating-bilateral-edge-no.tldr: RGIB improves noisy-graph link prediction by jointly managing corruption in graph structure and training labels.

paragraphs: Representing brain connectivity as a graph gives researchers access to structural and positional information for machine learning and network analysis. Building these graphs from MRI images, however, requires substantial computation and specialized preprocessing choices. The paper addresses this practical barrier by preparing a collection of functional brain networks for other researchers to use.

The authors gather MRI images from public databases and a private source, then work with domain experts to choose and apply the preprocessing steps. The resulting collection includes 2,702 subjects from six sources and covers four brain conditions. Providing processed graphs makes these data more directly accessible to researchers working at the intersection of neuroscience and graph learning.

The paper evaluates 12 machine learning models to establish baselines and checks data quality using a recent graph analysis model. It also releases preprocessing details and code alongside the networks. These contributions support comparison and reuse, reducing the need for every research team to independently reconstruct the full MRI-to-network workflow.
neurips-2023-data-driven-network-neurosc.tldr: A released collection of brain networks and preprocessing code lowers the barrier to machine learning research on MRI-derived connectivity.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a general-purpose neural network can learn visual reasoning directly from images without an explicit object-detection stage. The central issue is compositional generalization: using learned visual knowledge in new combinations. Success would challenge the view that a separately designed visual abstraction step is essential for this ability.

The authors propose self-supervised video pretraining. A transformer compresses each frame into a small collection of tokens and uses this compressed temporal context to reconstruct other frames. This objective encourages compact image representations while requiring the network to capture changes over time and object permanence, the persistence of objects through changes in what is visible.

Evaluations on CATER and ACRE show that pretraining is essential for compositional generalization in the studied end-to-end setup. The proposed approach substantially outperforms supervised pretraining based on image classification or explicit object detection. These findings support temporal reconstruction as a useful preparation for visual reasoning, with the evidence grounded in the two evaluated benchmarks.
neurips-2023-does-visual-pretraining-hel.tldr: Self-supervised video reconstruction enables strong end-to-end visual reasoning and outperforms supervised visual pretraining on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Visual explanations often identify the pixels that matter for a neural network's decision. Those maps can be difficult to interpret and sensitive to explanation errors. Explaining a decision through recognizable image regions offers another option, but earlier concept-based methods often depend on human annotations or a fixed vocabulary of concepts.

Explain Any Concept, or EAC, uses the Segment Anything Model to automatically obtain candidate concepts from the image being explained. This connects instance segmentation with concept-based explanation, allowing the explanatory units to come from the input itself. The approach aims to make explanations more flexible while reducing dependence on manually prepared concept collections.

Integrating Segment Anything into an explanation pipeline is computationally costly. The authors therefore introduce a lightweight per-input equivalent scheme that uses a surrogate model for efficient explanation. Evaluations on ImageNet and COCO report encouraging performance relative to commonly used explanation methods. The paper's contribution joins automatic concept preparation with an efficiency mechanism, addressing both how explanatory concepts are obtained and how they are used.
neurips-2023-explain-any-concept-segment.tldr: EAC uses Segment Anything to obtain image-specific concepts and a lightweight surrogate to explain visual model decisions efficiently.

paragraphs: Certified robustness concerns guarantees about a model's behavior under input perturbations. Deep equilibrium models have been less well understood in this respect than explicit networks. This paper studies that gap through Lipschitz constraints, which prescribe bounds on how strongly a network's outputs can change as its inputs change.

The central result connects several existing network structures to Lipschitz-bounded equilibrium networks, or LBEN. Convex potential, SDP-based Lipschitz, almost orthogonal, and Sandwich layers, along with monotone deep equilibrium models, can all be reparameterized as special cases of LBEN. Crucially, these transformations preserve the originally prescribed Lipschitz constant, retaining the constraint that makes the structures relevant to robustness.

This shared representation opens a route to improving equilibrium models through reparameterization, structure-preserving regularization, and LBEN-based fine-tuning. Classification experiments show improved certified robust accuracy using the proposed method. The theoretical contribution establishes connections while preserving Lipschitz prescriptions; the experiments demonstrate that those connections can be useful for improving certified performance in practice.
neurips-2023-exploiting-connections-betw.tldr: Reparameterizing several Lipschitz-constrained architectures as equilibrium networks preserves their bounds and supports improved certified robustness.

paragraphs: Recommendation fairness across item groups is often assessed by comparing how frequently each group is shown. This captures direct exposure but misses what can happen afterward. An item shown to a socially influential user may gain additional attention through sharing, so similar exposure counts can coexist with different opportunities for social reach.

The paper introduces two fairness metrics that account for the social attributes of users receiving recommendations. They require those attributes to be similar across the audiences exposed to different item groups. The authors then formulate recommendation training as a multi-objective optimization problem, allowing the balance between direct exposure utility and social utility to vary while controlling accuracy.

A gradient-based algorithm solves this formulation. The authors theoretically show that it can find Pareto-optimal solutions with different trade-offs and guaranteed accuracy: improving one objective cannot simply be achieved without sacrificing another at such a solution. Experiments on two real-world datasets support the approach. The contribution broadens fairness assessment to include who receives an exposure and its possible social consequences.
neurips-2023-fairly-recommending-with-so.tldr: The paper makes recommendation fairness sensitive to users' social attributes and provides controllable trade-offs between exposure, social utility, and accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper connects a frozen text-only language model with pretrained image encoders and decoders. Its central idea is to translate between their representation spaces, allowing existing language and visual models to work together. The resulting system accepts interleaved images and text and can respond with text, retrieved images, or newly generated images.

For image generation, an efficient mapping network translates the language model's hidden representations into the embedding space expected by an existing text-to-image model. This gives visual generation access to the language model's handling of complex textual context. A separate learned decision module uses the language model's representations to choose whether to generate an image or retrieve one from a predetermined dataset.

The authors report stronger generation performance than baseline models on tasks involving longer, more complex language, and improvements over non-LLM generators on several context-dependent tasks. These results support using a language model as a coordinator for multimodal inputs and outputs. The contribution includes both generating visual content and selecting an appropriate output mode during inference.
neurips-2023-generating-images-with-mult.tldr: Learned mappings connect a frozen language model to visual models for contextual image generation, retrieval, and multimodal dialogue.

paragraphs: Text-guided image segmentation must decide which pixels correspond to a description, but scenes admit several valid levels of detail. A description can refer to a broad semantic region, an individual object, or one of its parts. The paper treats this ambiguity as something the model should learn to represent explicitly.

HIPIE combines hierarchical representations with open-vocabulary and universal segmentation in one framework. It introduces a decoupled mechanism for combining text and image information, together with representation-learning modules for discrete objects, called things, and broader regions, called stuff. The authors also investigate how textual and visual features differ between these two category types.

Evaluations span ADE20K, COCO, Pascal-VOC Part, and RefCOCO/RefCOCOg. The authors report state-of-the-art results across semantic, instance, and part-level tasks, including segmentation and object detection. These findings support learning across multiple semantic levels within a shared system. The approach matters because it makes variation in the granularity of a requested region part of the learning problem itself.
neurips-2023-hierarchical-open-vocabular.tldr: HIPIE learns hierarchical visual representations to handle text-guided segmentation across semantic regions, individual objects, and their parts.

paragraphs: Code-generation benchmarks judge programs using test cases, so their conclusions depend on how thoroughly those tests exercise behavior. A program can pass a small test suite while still implementing the requested function incorrectly. This paper investigates how insufficient testing affects reported language-model performance and even the ordering of competing models.

EvalPlus expands an existing benchmark using automatic test-input generation that combines language-model and mutation-based strategies. The authors apply it to HumanEval, increasing its test cases eightyfold to create HumanEval+. This changes the scrutiny applied to generated programs, allowing the evaluation to uncover errors that the original tests missed.

Across 26 language models, the expanded tests detect substantial amounts of previously accepted incorrect code and reduce reported pass@k scores. Rankings also change: WizardCoder-CodeLlama and Phind-CodeLlama outperform ChatGPT on HumanEval+, despite neither doing so on HumanEval. The results show that benchmark test coverage can materially affect conclusions about code-generation ability. The released tools, datasets, and generated programs support further work on automated benchmark improvement.
neurips-2023-is-your-code-generated-by-c.tldr: EvalPlus exposes previously missed errors in generated code and shows that stronger tests can change model rankings.

paragraphs: Formal theorem proving requires selecting useful mathematical premises as well as constructing proof steps. Research has also faced practical barriers from private datasets, unavailable code, and demanding training requirements. LeanDojo supplies an open environment with tools, data, models, and benchmarks for studying language-model theorem proving in Lean.

The system extracts proof data and supports programmatic interaction with Lean. Detailed annotations identify premises used in proofs, enabling the authors to train ReProver, a language-model prover with retrieval from a large mathematical library. Program analysis helps the retriever identify available premises and difficult negative examples. The reported training requirement is one GPU week.

A benchmark contains 98,734 theorems and proofs, including a challenging split where evaluation proofs rely on premises never used during training. This tests whether the prover can use newly relevant library material. Experiments show ReProver outperforming non-retrieval baselines and GPT-4. Together, the retrieval method and openly released infrastructure make premise selection more effective and the research workflow easier to reproduce.
neurips-2023-leandojo-theorem-proving-wi.tldr: LeanDojo provides open theorem-proving infrastructure, while ReProver improves proof generation by retrieving relevant mathematical premises.

paragraphs: Large language models are expensive to deploy, run, and train because of their size. Compressing them is challenging when the goal is to retain broad language and multitask abilities rather than optimize for one narrow application. The paper also seeks to minimize dependence on the enormous datasets used for original model training.

LLM-Pruner removes coupled model structures judged less critical using gradient information. This structural pruning aims to retain as much functionality as possible while reducing the model. Because deleting structures can damage performance, the method follows pruning with LoRA tuning to recover capability. The authors report recovery in three hours using 50K data.

The evaluation covers LLaMA, Vicuna, and ChatGLM. The compressed models retain what the authors describe as satisfactory zero-shot classification and generation capabilities. These findings support a task-agnostic compression workflow combining selective structural removal with relatively limited recovery training. The stated objective is preservation of general usefulness under reduced data dependence, rather than compression tailored to a particular downstream task.
neurips-2023-llm-pruner-on-the-structura.tldr: LLM-Pruner combines gradient-guided structural pruning with LoRA recovery to compress language models while retaining broad capabilities.

paragraphs: First-person videos of human activity contain useful demonstrations for robots, but hands obscure objects and look different from robot end-effectors. Simply removing the hand also discards information about the action. The paper proposes separating the human agent and the environment into a factored representation that preserves both sources of information.

Its central component, Video Inpainting via Diffusion Model, reconstructs obscured scene content using two kinds of evidence. A large pretrained diffusion model supplies a prior over real-world images, while attention draws on how the object appeared in earlier video frames. These complementary signals help fill regions hidden by the hand while supporting the separation of agent and environment.

Experiments show improved inpainting quality in egocentric videos and demonstrate the usefulness of the resulting representation for multiple robotics-related tasks. These include object detection, reconstruction of manipulated objects in 3D, and learning rewards, policies, and affordances from video. The approach makes hand-related information and environmental information separately available, easing the design of downstream models.
neurips-2023-look-ma-no-hands-agent-envi.tldr: Separating hands from their environment preserves action information while diffusion-based inpainting improves the scene representation for robotics tasks.

paragraphs: A visually controlled agent may learn a task from a limited set of camera views and struggle when the viewpoint changes. The paper studies this problem of view generalization, organizing it into four challenging scenarios intended to resemble situations that arise in practice. This gives the evaluation a broader scope than a single type of view change.

MoVie adapts visual model-based policies at test time. The proposed approach requires neither explicit reward signals during adaptation nor modifications to the original training process. These properties address a practical deployment problem: an already trained agent encounters unfamiliar views and needs to adjust without receiving task rewards that directly score its behavior.

Experiments cover 18 tasks from DMControl, xArm, and Adroit across the four scenarios. The authors report relative improvements of 33%, 86%, and 152% for these three task sources, respectively. The results support the effectiveness of test-time adaptation in the evaluated settings and suggest potential for robotics applications where the deployment viewpoint differs from those available during training.
neurips-2023-movie-visual-model-based-po.tldr: MoVie adapts visual model-based policies to unfamiliar views at test time without explicit rewards or training changes.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a linear decision boundary when inputs follow a Gaussian distribution and labels contain random classification noise. The boundary may have an offset, so it need not pass through the origin. The central question is how much data learning requires, and how that answer changes when computation must be efficient.

The authors establish that the information-theoretic sample requirement scales as d/ε up to logarithmic factors, where d is the dimension and ε is excess error. They also give an efficient algorithm whose data requirement depends on the target halfspace's bias. This makes the geometry of the target part of the computational learning picture.

On the lower-bound side, efficient statistical-query algorithms or low-degree tests require at least Ω(√d/max(p, ε)²) samples, with p measuring target bias. The nearly matching results reveal a gap between having enough information and learning efficiently. The lower bound suggests quadratic dependence on inverse error is inherent for efficient algorithms, while its formal scope concerns the specified computational frameworks.
neurips-2023-near-optimal-bounds-for-lea.tldr: The paper reveals an information–computation gap for learning Gaussian halfspaces with random label noise through algorithmic and restricted-model lower bounds.

paragraphs: Some machine learning objectives depend on a neural network's derivatives as well as its output values. Understanding such objectives requires mathematical control over the complexity of the derivative functions the network can represent. This paper develops nearly optimal estimates of that complexity using VC-dimension and pseudo-dimension, two measures of function-class capacity.

The estimates have two stated applications. First, they support a nearly tight approximation result in Sobolev space, where approximation concerns derivatives alongside function values. Second, they characterize generalization error for learning methods whose losses involve derivatives. These applications connect the expressive possibilities of neural networks with questions about their behavior beyond the training data.

The work supplies theoretical learning-error estimates relevant to a broad range of physics-informed methods. The abstract names partial differential equations, operator learning, generative models, compression, distillation, and regularization among the applications. Its contribution is mathematical support for analyzing derivative-dependent learning, providing complexity bounds for a quantity that ordinary output-focused analysis does not directly characterize.
neurips-2023-nearly-optimal-vc-dimension.tldr: Nearly optimal complexity bounds for neural-network derivatives support approximation and generalization analysis for derivative-dependent learning.

paragraphs: Neuro-symbolic systems combine neural perception with logical reasoning, but learning the two components together remains challenging. Neural networks operate with continuous quantities, while logical constraints make discrete distinctions. This paper proposes a unified training process that learns neural parameters, connects observations to symbols, and synthesizes logical constraints.

The framework uses difference-of-convex programming to relax logical constraints while preserving their precision. It represents learnable rules through cardinality constraints, which express restrictions on how many conditions hold. A trust-region method helps prevent the logical constraints from degenerating during learning. Together, these techniques address both the continuous–discrete mismatch and the stability of the learned logical component.

The authors attribute the framework's capability to improved interaction between neural and symbolic components during both training and inference. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation support its effectiveness. The contribution is a coherent mechanism for learning perception and constraints jointly, so the symbolic component participates in the learning process alongside the neural network and remains relevant when the system makes predictions.
neurips-2023-neuro-symbolic-learning-yie.tldr: A unified neuro-symbolic framework jointly learns neural representations, symbol grounding, and logical constraints through continuous optimization.

paragraphs: Predicting a dynamic system's future state requires accounting for how it changes over the intervening time. Graph neural networks have achieved accurate predictions even for distant future states. This paper examines a shared structure beneath otherwise different approaches to modeling system coordinates and interacting forces.

The authors show that these approaches can be viewed as learning an integral of velocity between initial and final coordinates. In the methods they analyze, however, the integrated quantity is constant with respect to time. Their proposed approach instead combines several velocity estimates using Newton–Cotes formulas, allowing the integration calculation to incorporate more than one estimate across the interval.

The paper provides a theoretical argument for the method's effectiveness and reports consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on several benchmarks. The contribution concerns how learned velocity information becomes a prediction of future coordinates. By revisiting that integration step, the authors identify a shared simplification in existing designs and provide a numerically motivated way to improve dynamic prediction.
neurips-2023-newtoncotes-graph-neural-ne.tldr: Newton–Cotes graph networks improve dynamic-system prediction by integrating several velocity estimates instead of a time-constant integrand.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine repeated probability forecasts from multiple experts. At each time step, experts provide distributions over possible outcomes, and the learner chooses how much weight to give each expert. The aggregation rule is logarithmic pooling, which combines forecasts through weighted log odds and is evaluated using logarithmic loss.

The aim is to learn weights whose cumulative loss stays close to that of the best fixed weights chosen after all outcomes are known. The setting permits adversarial forecasts and outcomes, but imposes a necessary consistency condition: experts must report calibrated forecasts. This creates a semi-adversarial problem that retains substantial adversarial flexibility while restricting which sequences are allowed.

Using online mirror descent, the authors obtain expected regret of O(√T log T) over T rounds. Since this grows more slowly than T, the expected regret per round tends toward zero. The result establishes a no-regret guarantee for logarithmic pooling in the stated calibrated setting, despite the difficulty posed by unbounded losses.
neurips-2023-no-regret-learning-with-unb.tldr: An online mirror-descent method learns logarithmic-pooling weights with sublinear expected regret under a calibration constraint on expert forecasts.

paragraphs: Navigation agents that follow language instructions need varied visual environments for training, but photorealistic environments are scarce. PanoGen addresses this bottleneck by generating panoramic environments from text descriptions. The goal is to expand training diversity so agents can better handle places they have not previously encountered.

The method captions room images from Matterport3D and uses those descriptions to condition a text-to-image diffusion model. Recursive outpainting extends generated images into consistent 360-degree panoramas. Text conditioning preserves similar semantic content, while outpainting introduces variation in room appearance and layout. The generated environments are used both to create instruction-and-path data for pretraining and to augment visual observations during fine-tuning.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on Room-to-Room, Room-for-Room, and CVDN. Generated instruction data is especially effective for CVDN, whose underspecified instructions require commonsense knowledge. Agents also benefit from additional generated panoramas. These findings support the potential of scaling synthetic environments, while the possibility of generating indefinitely many environments remains a capacity claim rather than a demonstrated training scale.
neurips-2023-panogen-text-conditioned-pa.tldr: PanoGen creates text-conditioned panoramas that improve language-guided navigation training and generalization in the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Combining different data modalities can give a model complementary information, but dependencies and confounding factors across sources can also introduce unwanted variability and bias. The paper focuses on preparing features before modalities are fused, where normalization can address these effects before they influence the combined representation.

RegBN is a multimodal batch-normalization method that uses a Frobenius-norm regularizer to address confounders and dependencies among data sources. It works with both low-level and high-level features and requires no learnable parameters. This design simplifies its contribution to training and inference while allowing it to be applied at different stages of a multimodal network.

The authors validate RegBN on eight databases spanning five research areas. The modalities include language, audio, images, video, depth, tabular data, and 3D MRI. Evaluations also cover multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and vision transformers. This breadth supports the method's applicability across different data combinations and architectures, with normalization serving as a common intervention before heterogeneous information is fused.
neurips-2023-regbn-batch-normalization-o.tldr: RegBN normalizes multimodal features with regularization to address cross-source dependencies and confounding without adding learnable parameters.

paragraphs: Language-model representations can help predict brain responses to natural language. This paper asks whether increasing model size improves those predictions, extending investigation beyond models around GPT-2's scale. The authors test larger open-source models, including OPT and LLaMA, against brain responses measured with fMRI.

Across models ranging from 125 million to 30 billion parameters, prediction performance grows approximately logarithmically with model size. The authors report about a 15% improvement in encoding performance, measured through correlation on held-out data across three subjects. Increasing the fMRI training-data volume produces similar log-linear behavior. Acoustic encoding models using HuBERT, WavLM, and Whisper also improve with model size.

A noise-ceiling analysis indicates that the strongest models approach the theoretical maximum performance for some regions, including the precuneus and higher auditory cortex. These findings suggest that larger models and datasets can improve models of brain language processing. The evidence describes predictive relationships and region-specific ceilings, supporting potential scientific and decoding applications without establishing that the models reproduce every aspect of brain computation.
neurips-2023-scaling-laws-for-language-e.tldr: Larger language models and more fMRI training data improve brain-response prediction approximately logarithmically in the studied settings.

paragraphs: Circuit designers repeatedly analyze how signals travel through interconnects, making both prediction accuracy and computational speed valuable. Interconnects can be represented as trees of resistances and capacitances. SyncTREE uses this structure to build a specialized graph neural network for timing analysis that incorporates circuit topology and physical properties.

The model passes information through the tree in two directions: bottom-up and top-down. This produces graph representations informed by both directions of the structure. A tree contrastive loss guides representation learning, and a closed-formula-based component supports fast timing calculations. These elements tailor the model to the particular organization and physical behavior of interconnects.

Experiments use real integrated-circuit design data and compare predictions against industry reference numerical analyses. Among the conventional graph neural network models evaluated, SyncTREE produces the best predictions for signal delays and slews, which describe transition timing. The findings support using the tree structure and circuit physics together when designing learned timing models for repeated analysis during the circuit-design process.
neurips-2023-synctree-fast-timing-analys.tldr: SyncTREE combines circuit physics with bidirectional tree message passing to improve interconnect timing predictions on real circuit-design data.
